options.why: Keeping 18 months of data entirely on hot, typically EBS-backed and replicated storage is the most expensive way to satisfy retention. This ignores UltraWarm and cold tiering, which exist specifically to make older data affordable to keep searchable.

options.text: Send logs to CloudWatch Logs and run all queries, both recent and 18-month-old, with CloudWatch Logs Insights.
options.why: Logs Insights is priced per GB scanned per query and works well for ad hoc troubleshooting of recent logs, but repeatedly scanning full-text queries across 18 months of retained data at 2 TB/day scale becomes expensive, and it does not provide fuzzy/relevance search or rich built-in dashboarding.

options.text: Store logs in S3 and query them with Amazon Athena using its built-in interface for visualization.
options.why: Athena runs SQL well over structured or semi-structured data in S3, but it has no inverted index for full-text or fuzzy search, cannot deliver sub-second interactive search, and has no built-in dashboarding -- a separate BI tool would be needed.

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service with hot nodes for the most recent logs, UltraWarm for the several-months range, and the cold storage tier for the oldest retained data, visualized with OpenSearch Dashboards.
options.why: OpenSearch provides full-text and fuzzy search through an inverted index with sub-second response on hot nodes. UltraWarm attaches S3-backed storage at a much lower cost per GB while keeping data queryable, and the cold tier further reduces cost for rarely accessed indices that can be reattached on demand. OpenSearch Dashboards provides the built-in visualization the security team wants.

questions.knowledge_point: OpenSearch Service tiers by access recency: hot (fast, expensive), UltraWarm (S3-backed, cheaper, still queryable, best for infrequently accessed but searchable data), and cold (cheapest, indices detached and reattached on demand). It fits full-text/fuzzy search plus built-in dashboards. CloudWatch Logs Insights suits ad hoc troubleshooting of recent logs; Athena suits SQL analytics over S3, not full-text relevance search.
questions.trap_alert: Seeing '18 months of logs' and assuming cost forces a move to S3 plus Athena. Athena cannot do full-text or fuzzy search or built-in dashboards -- UltraWarm and cold tiers let OpenSearch keep that data searchable at far lower cost than all-hot storage.
questions.mnemonic: Hot = fast and pricey. UltraWarm = S3-backed and still searchable. Cold = cheapest, dormant until reattached.

questions.scenario: A financial-services company built a data lake in S3 that is queried by Amazon Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and Amazon EMR, used by separate risk, marketing, and finance teams. Compliance requires that marketing analysts can query customer transaction tables but never see name or national ID columns, and that finance analysts see only rows for their own business unit. Access today is managed through a growing patchwork of S3 bucket policies and per-service IAM policies that regularly drift out of sync between the consuming services.
questions.stem: Which change provides centralized, fine-grained (column- and row-level) access control that is consistently enforced across all three query engines with the LEAST ongoing administrative overhead?

options.text: Register the S3 locations with AWS Lake Formation and define column-level and row-level grants (using data filters) on the Glue Data Catalog tables for each team, so Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR all enforce the same permissions.
options.why: Lake Formation centralizes data-lake permissions at the Glue Data Catalog level, down to specific columns and rows via data filters. Every Lake Formation-integrated engine reads and enforces the same grant, so Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR stay in sync automatically without separate per-service policy maintenance.

options.text: Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate least-privilege policies per team and attach them directly to each team's IAM role for the Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR services in use.
options.why: IAM Access Analyzer helps identify overly permissive policies and generate policies based on observed access activity, but it has no concept of column- or row-level filtering within a shared table, and separate IAM policies per service would still need manual synchronization across three engines.

options.text: Create separate masked or filtered copies of each table for each team, refreshed nightly by an AWS Glue ETL job.
options.why: Maintaining per-team (and per-business-unit, for row filtering) copies of data multiplies storage and ETL pipelines that must be kept current -- exactly the high ongoing administrative overhead the requirement is trying to eliminate, compared to a single centrally managed set of grants.

options.text: Write separate S3 bucket policies scoped to each team's prefix, plus IAM policies restricting each service's role to specific columns using S3 Select.
options.why: S3 bucket policies and IAM policies operate at the object/resource level, not aware of columns or rows inside a table's data, and S3 Select filters what a single request returns rather than serving as a manageable, catalog-level permission model. This is essentially the existing patchwork approach the company is already struggling with.

questions.knowledge_point: AWS Lake Formation centralizes data-lake permissions at the Glue Data Catalog layer -- grant or revoke once, down to column and row (via data filters) -- and every Lake Formation-integrated engine (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR with Lake Formation support) enforces the same grants, eliminating per-service IAM/bucket-policy patchwork and drift.
questions.trap_alert: Reaching for 'more IAM policies' or 'more S3 bucket policies' whenever access requirements tighten. Neither is column- or row-aware inside shared tables, and both require separate upkeep per consuming service -- the discriminator here is centralized, fine-grained control enforced consistently across multiple engines, which is specifically Lake Formation's job.
questions.mnemonic: Lake Formation: one grant, every engine obeys. IAM/bucket policies: per-service, per-object, no column or row awareness.

questions.scenario: A retail application backed by RDS MySQL has a small set of product-catalog keys read thousands of times per second but updated only a few times per day. The team is adding ElastiCache in front of RDS to reduce read load. They can tolerate up to 5 minutes of staleness after a product update, want cache misses to self-populate transparently without extra write-path complexity, and want to avoid an ever-growing cache holding data nobody has read in a long time.
questions.stem: Which two elements of the caching strategy meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set a TTL of 5 minutes on cached items so they expire and are reloaded lazily from RDS.
options.why: A TTL matching the 5-minute staleness tolerance bounds how stale cached product data can be, and expired keys are evicted automatically, capping how long unread or stale data lingers -- working together with lazy loading.

options.text: Lazy loading (cache-aside): the application checks the cache first, and on a miss reads from RDS and populates the cache.
options.why: Lazy loading only ever populates the cache with data that was actually requested, and it self-populates on a miss without any additional logic on the write path, matching the requirement to add caching transparently.

options.text: Configure read-through caching using an AWS-managed connector between ElastiCache and RDS that automatically loads missed keys from the database.
options.why: Unlike DAX for DynamoDB, ElastiCache has no built-in managed read-through connector to RDS. Achieving read-through behavior for ElastiCache in front of RDS requires implementing the fetch-on-miss logic in the application, which in practice is the same as lazy loading -- there is no separate managed mechanism to select here.

options.text: Disable eviction entirely and size the cache node to hold the full catalog forever.
options.why: Disabling eviction means keys stay resident indefinitely regardless of the staleness requirement or whether they are still being read, directly contradicting the goal of avoiding an ever-growing cache and providing no staleness bound at all.

options.text: Write-through: every write to RDS is immediately mirrored into the cache by the application.
options.why: Write-through requires extra logic on every write path and pre-populates the cache with data that may never be read, growing the cache with unused entries -- the opposite of what the team wants to avoid, and it adds write-path complexity they explicitly want to skip.

questions.knowledge_point: Lazy loading (cache-aside) caches only requested data and self-populates on miss with minimal write-path change; pairing it with a TTL bounds staleness to a tolerance and evicts stale or unused entries. Write-through adds write-path complexity and pre-populates possibly-unused data. ElastiCache has no native managed read-through/write-through connector to RDS -- that pattern belongs to DAX for DynamoDB.
questions.trap_alert: Assuming 'read-through' is an off-the-shelf ElastiCache-plus-RDS feature comparable to DAX for DynamoDB. For RDS, lazy loading combined with a TTL, both handled in application/client code, is the standard combination -- there is no managed connector to pick.
questions.mnemonic: Lazy load = only what's asked for. TTL = a staleness leash. Write-through = write twice, cache everything whether it's read or not.

questions.scenario: An HPC research team runs a tightly-coupled MPI simulation across a cluster of c6i instances placed in a cluster placement group within a single Availability Zone. The workload is latency-sensitive and depends on OS-bypass communication between nodes to hit its target simulation throughput. All instances communicate only with each other inside the same VPC.
questions.stem: Which two configuration choices should the team make to maximize inter-node network performance for this workload? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set the MTU on all instances to 9001 bytes (jumbo frames), since traffic stays entirely within the VPC.
options.why: Jumbo frames at 9001 MTU are supported for traffic that stays inside the VPC (including intra-Region VPC peering), reducing per-packet overhead for the large volumes of intra-VPC traffic this MPI workload generates.

options.text: Set the MTU to 8500 bytes across all instances, matching the AWS Direct Connect jumbo frame limit.
options.why: 8500 MTU is the jumbo frame ceiling for traffic traversing an AWS Direct Connect connection, not for instance-to-instance traffic within the same VPC, which supports the full 9001 MTU.

options.text: Attach an Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) to each instance alongside its standard ENA interface, and use an MPI library that supports EFA's OS-bypass capability.
options.why: EFA provides OS-bypass hardware interfaces built for HPC and tightly-coupled MPI workloads running in a cluster placement group, cutting inter-node latency and jitter beyond what standard networking alone can achieve.

options.text: Set the MTU on all instances to 1500 bytes, since that is the standard recommendation for cluster placement groups.
options.why: 1500 MTU is the ceiling for traffic leaving the VPC over the public internet or a Site-to-Site VPN, not the setting for intra-VPC HPC traffic -- this is exactly the case where jumbo frames should be used instead.

options.text: Rely on the standard Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) alone, tuned with enhanced networking, as a substitute for EFA for MPI collective operations.
options.why: Standard ENA delivers high bandwidth and enhanced networking but does not provide OS-bypass. Tightly-coupled MPI collective operations that need the lowest possible latency are the specific use case EFA exists for, and ENA alone cannot deliver it.

questions.knowledge_point: EFA adds OS-bypass hardware interfaces on top of ENA for latency-sensitive, tightly-coupled HPC/MPI workloads in a cluster placement group. MTU ceilings: 9001 (jumbo frames) for intra-VPC / same-Region VPC peering traffic, 8500 over Direct Connect, and 1500 over the public internet or Site-to-Site VPN.
questions.trap_alert: Defaulting to 1500 MTU as 'the standard' regardless of path. The scenario states traffic never leaves the VPC, which is precisely when 9001 jumbo frames apply -- using 1500 there wastes throughput on unnecessary packet overhead.
questions.mnemonic: 9001 inside the VPC, 8500 through Direct Connect, 1500 out to the internet. EFA is ENA plus OS-bypass for HPC.
